Warning signs of grooming

• A new older "friend" met in a game or app
• Gifts, game currency or money you can't explain
• Being asked to move a chat to another app, keep secrets or send photos
• Hiding the screen, using the phone late at night
• Seeming anxious, withdrawn or upset after being online
If something feels wrong

• Stay calm and thank them for telling you: they are not in trouble.
• Don't delete anything: take screenshots of chats and usernames.
• Block and report the account in the app.
• Never pay or send more images if someone is threatening to share photos.
• Report it: NCMEC CyberTipline (US), CEOP (UK) or your local police. Take It Down (takeitdown.ncmec.org) helps remove nude images of under-18s.
How this works

Perfsentient compares the apps installed on this phone with a built-in list of apps that child-safety organisations, regulators and investigations have raised concerns about. Suggested ages combine each app\'s own terms, its Google Play content rating and guidance from groups such as Common Sense Media, eSafety and the NSPCC. It is a guide, not a verdict: you know your child best. Nothing leaves this phone.
Game with open chat
Players can chat, talk and trade with people they don\'t know. Groomers use games to befriend children, offer gifts or game currency, and then move the chat to a private app.

• Use the game's parental controls to turn off chat or limit it to friends.
• Play together sometimes and ask who they talk to.
• Agree that people met in a game don't get other usernames, photos or where they live.
• Require approval or set a limit for purchases.
Avatar world or social VR
Users meet as avatars in shared rooms with voice and text chat. Investigations found adults, sexual role-play and private rooms where children can be isolated.

• Check the age setting and turn on any teen or junior mode.
• Limit voice chat and private messages to friends.
• Keep headsets and phones in shared rooms.
• Talk about what to do if someone asks them to go somewhere private.
Social media

Feeds built to keep scrolling, with messages and comments from strangers. Australia bans accounts under 16 on the largest platforms, and sextortion gangs mostly approach teens through Instagram and Snapchat.

• Make the account private and limit messages to people they follow.
• Use the app's teen account or family supervision tools.
• Turn off location in posts.
• Agree on screen-time limits and keep phones out of bedrooms at night.
Private messaging
Private, encrypted or disappearing chats. This is where groomers and sextortion scammers try to move a conversation that started somewhere else.

• Allow messages and group invites from contacts or friends only.
• Turn off location sharing (for example Ghost Mode on Snap Map).
• Use family supervision tools where they exist, such as Snapchat or Discord Family Center.
• Make it clear they can always tell you if someone asks for photos or secrecy, without losing their phone.
Friend-finding or swipe app
Swipe to meet strangers, often nearby. Works like a dating app for teens and is a known starting point for sextortion.

• Ask why they want to meet new people and look at the app together.
• Turn off location and hide the profile from people nearby.
• Never move a chat to another app or send photos to someone met here.
• Consider removing it: there is no truly safe "Tinder for teens".
Random video chat
Connects to random strangers on live video. Meant for adults, with frequent nudity and no reliable age checks.

• These apps aren\'t suitable for children: remove it.\n• Talk calmly about what they may have seen, and don\'t punish honesty.\n• If they were asked to do something sexual on camera, keep the evidence and report it.
Anonymous messages and Q&A
Lets people send anonymous questions and messages, which makes bullying easy. US regulators acted against NGL and Sendit, including for sending teens fake messages.
• Talk about how anonymous messages can be cruel, and are sometimes fake.\n• Check for paid \"see who sent this\" subscriptions.\n• Consider removing it, especially after hurtful messages.
Live streaming
Broadcast live to strangers who can comment and send paid gifts. Gifts and attention are used to pressure young streamers into doing more on camera.

• Don't let younger children stream publicly; keep streams to friends.
• Turn off gifts, payouts and private messages where possible.
• Never stream from a bedroom or show their school or address.
• Set a spending limit for virtual coins.
Adult dating app
For adults only (18+). Matches people nearby and is used to arrange sexual contact.

• A child shouldn\'t have this app: remove it.\n• Calmly find out how they came to use it and who they talked to.\n• If an adult contacted them sexually, keep the messages and report it to the police.
AI companion or role-play bot
AI characters that act as friends or partners. Testing by Common Sense Media and Stanford found sexual role-play and harmful advice; they recommend no use under 18.

• Explain that the characters aren\'t real and can be wrong or manipulative.\n• Watch for late-night use and pulling away from real friends.\n• Consider removing it. If they are struggling, help them find a real person to talk to.
Secret vault or app hider
Hides photos, videos, chats or other apps, often disguised as a calculator. It can be harmless privacy, but it is also used to hide contact with strangers or images used for sextortion.

• Talk about it openly rather than secretly searching it.\n• Ask what they want to keep private and why.\n• Make sure they know they won\'t be in trouble for telling you if someone is pressuring them for images.
Gambling or casino game
Real-money betting or casino-style games. Gambling young raises the risk of gambling problems later in life.

• Real-money betting is not allowed for minors: remove it and check for linked payment cards.\n• For casino-style games, block in-app purchases.\n• Talk about how these games are designed to keep you playing.
Filter bypass tool
Routes traffic around network filters and parental controls, and opens hidden websites, some of which host illegal content.
• Ask what they use it for: privacy is a fair reason for older teens.\n• Check whether your parental controls still work while it is installed.\n• For younger children, remove it.
Grooming cases
Police, courts or child-safety groups have documented adults grooming children here.
Sextortion
Named in research and law-enforcement warnings about criminals who trick teens into sharing images and then blackmail them.
Legal action
Sued, investigated by regulators or pulled from app stores over child safety.
Adult content
Sexual or other adult content is easy to find or is sent by other users.
Strangers
People your child doesn\'t know can message, call or play with them.
Live video
Live video with people your child doesn\'t know. It isn\'t checked before it is shown.
Anonymous
Users don\'t need a real identity, so it is hard to know who is on the other side.
Disappearing messages
Messages vanish after being seen, so there is nothing to look back at.
Location
Can show where your child is or match them with people nearby.
Bullying
Known for anonymous abuse and pile-ons.
AI role-play
AI characters act as friends or partners and can hold sexual or harmful conversations.
Hides content
Hides photos, chats or other apps behind a disguise or PIN.
Bypasses controls
Can get around parental controls or network filters.
Gambling
Real-money betting or casino-style games.
Violence
Realistic violence and weapons.
In-app spending
Virtual currency, gifts or loot boxes bought with real money. Gifts are also a grooming tactic.
Endless feed
Built to keep scrolling, which can crowd out sleep and offline time.
